subject: hedgehog
pitch: A plump hedgehog out on an autumn evening walk. A dome of spines in chestnut brown with cream tips, a soft fawn face with a pointed, twitchy snout, a shiny black button nose, tiny round ears and bright beady eyes. Little pink paws, and a single red maple leaf stuck on its spines like a trophy.
reasoning:
I'm planning a stylized hedgehog model using the SDK, sizing it realistically at roughly 0.3 m long and 0.2 m tall to match a plump, rounded look.

For the structure, I'm figuring out the joint hierarchy for a quadruped-style body and deciding how to construct the spines — scattering a few hundred small cone-shaped spikes across the dome of the body surface, keeping triangle counts low so performance stays reasonable within the part limit.

For color, I'm working out how to give each spine a chestnut base with a cream tip — since paints are model-space functions and can't easily target individual spikes, I'll build each spine as two stacked cones, a longer chestnut one topped with a short cream one, roughly doubling the mesh count but keeping the look simple.

I'm checking that using the surface-scatter stick function with cone geometry naturally orients each spine's apex outward along the surface normal, which is exactly the base-up orientation hedgehog spines need, though I still need to think through how to bias the scatter so spines read as swept-back rather than purely random.

Simpler to use explicit `bone` assignment for rigid attachment since the body is effectively one bone anyway — spines and body all move together. For the body shape itself, I'm thinking a squashed sphere (ellipsoid via scale) works well as the dome-like hedgehog form, colored as the underlying skin tone beneath the spines.

For the head and snout, I want a separate fawn-colored sphere with a tapered cone or spike shape pointing forward to form the pointed snout — comparing options like `spike` or a tapered `rod` with flat-to-point caps to get that pinched nose look.

Now I'm thinking through the leg rigging: short quadruped legs with pink paw tips, structured as named joint chains (hip, knee, foot) per leg so the skeleton can drive a simple rest pose.

Right, so with 3 names the tip count works out correctly. But I realize the joint creation logic needs the parent specified explicitly rather than relying on nearestJoint inference, since that could pick the wrong joint — I'll pass "body" as the parent directly.

Now I'm working out the actual skeleton structure: a root joint near the pelvis, then figuring out realistic hedgehog body dimensions (body length, width, height) to position everything proportionally.

Continuing, I'm setting the body ellipsoid center at y=0.085 with radii 0.075/0.07/0.105, legs bridging the ~0.015m gap to the ground, and pink paw ellipsoids sitting flush with y=0. Spines extend outward from the dome by about 0.035m, bringing total height to roughly 0.19m, and I need to make sure the spine coverage wraps the back/sides/rump while leaving the fawn-colored face and belly exposed.

Now I'm placing the head: a fawn sphere up front with a tapered snout rod extending forward to a small black nose, beady black eyes with tiny white catchlight highlights positioned on either side of the face, and tiny flattened round ears near the top.

For the leaf trophy stuck on the spines, I'm thinking a maple leaf shape with its characteristic five lobes, built either as an extruded flat outline or a textured card, keeping the color a simple red without overcomplicating with gradients or vein details.

Mapping out the leaf's outline point by point, working symmetrically from the stem up through the lower lobes to the central top lobe, mirroring the right half onto the left so the shape stays balanced.

I'm restructuring the top lobe so it has a clean notch-tip-notch pattern, then mirroring the right-half sequence to build the left side, giving roughly sixteen points total for stem, lower lobes, side lobes, and the top peak. I'm also double-checking the stem base forms a narrow triangle and that the point ordering stays consistent even though orientation itself doesn't matter here.

Checking the point sequence for self-intersections now — tracing each lobe edge against neighboring segments to confirm nothing overlaps on the right side or its mirrored left side. So far the path looks clean, with notches and tips staying properly separated in y-range, so I'm moving on to scaling the leaf shape.

Working out the right scale factor so the leaf comes out around 10cm wide like a real maple leaf, settling on roughly 0.075-0.08 for a trophy-sized piece. Now I'm figuring out the extrude function's orientation parameters — deciding how the leaf's x/y axes should map into model space so it faces the right direction when attached to the back, possibly tilting it with a rotated x-direction vector.

To actually sell the "stuck on spines" effect, I'm adding a thin stem rod connecting the leaf's base point down to the body surface, essentially a small stick impaling through, computed using the leaf's local coordinate transform to find the stem anchor point.

I'll simplify by having the leaf sit on top of the spine dome with a short stem rod anchoring it down into the spines, rather than overengineering the attachment. I'm settling on joint naming for the limbs: front legs use "shoulderL/R", "elbowL/R", "wristL/R", and hind legs use "hipL/R", "kneeL/R", "ankleL/R" so rigger-friendly names stay distinct between front and back without clashing.

Now I'm sizing the body and legs — bumping the body centre up with bottom around y=0.03, legs reaching down to the ground at y=0 so only a few centimeters show, keeping that plump stubby-legged hedgehog look, with paw ellipsoids resting right on the floor.

I'm also working out the overall proportions: body as an elongated ellipsoid, head overlapping the front, and a pointed snout extending forward, while trying to keep total length realistic for a hedgehog (around 0.25-0.3m) rather than letting it balloon too large.

The face itself should stay spine-free fawn-colored, with spines scattered only on the body surface starting behind the head junction -- I need to figure out the right z-cutoff so there isn't an awkward bare gap where the head sphere meets the body dome.

I also want to avoid putting spines on the underbelly, so I'm filtering by normal direction to keep them mostly on the sides and top, while estimating a reasonable spine count based on the available surface area after excluding the face and bottom regions.

To avoid z-fighting where the chestnut and cream cones would overlap at the same surface, I'll switch the chestnut base to a tapered cylinder (frustum) running up to 70% of the spine height, with the cream cone covering just the top 30% as its own separate piece.

For normals, I realize I need to pass flat: true so the geometry gets computeVertexNormals called on it after cloning the non-indexed buffer, giving faceted per-face shading that suits the low-poly spine look. For the surface normal orientation, I'm checking that the triangle winding from SphereGeometry is counter-clockwise viewed from outside, so the cross product of the transformed edges should still point outward even under non-uniform scaling, since it's proportional to the cofactor-transformed normal and preserves correct orientation as long as the determinant stays positive -- though I need to confirm this doesn't distort magnitude or direction in edge cases.

For spine placement, I'm using the hit's face normal blended with a backward tilt vector so spines fan outward and angle toward the rear, then positioning each spine's base slightly embedded into the surface along that direction to avoid visible gaps.

I'm also checking the buried-point logic: rays cast outward from surface points on the convex body should always escape cleanly, so points won't get falsely flagged as buried. Now I'm setting up the actual joint hierarchy: a root "body" joint, with a child "head" joint carrying the fawn snout sphere, and I'm considering whether the mouth needs separate upper and lower jaw parts so it can open and close like other rigged creatures.

For the snout, nose, and lower jaw I'm fitting tapered rod dimensions so the jaw hinge and mouth sit naturally beneath the snout without poking through visibly, accepting some overlap since it's a subtle stylized feature.
